claims.claim: The figurine was carved/left in the ground around 30,000 years ago
claims.quote: The figure itself is estimated to have been left in the ground around 30,000 years ago, based on radiocarbon dates from the layers surrounding it.

claims.claim: The figurine has no face — no eyes, mouth or nose
claims.quote: The figure has no visible face, her head being covered with circular horizontal bands of what might be rows of plaited hair, or perhaps a type of headdress.

claims.claim: It is 11.1 centimetres tall
claims.quote: The Venus of Willendorf is an 11.1-centimetre-tall (4.4 in) Venus figurine

claims.claim: It is made of oolitic limestone and tinted with red ochre
claims.quote: carved from an oolitic limestone that is not local to the area, and tinted with red ochre

claims.claim: The figurine is in the Naturhistorisches Museum Wien (Natural History Museum, Vienna)
claims.quote: It is in the Natural History Museum in Vienna, Austria as of 2003.

claims.claim: Rows of bands cover the head where a face should be

claims.quote: The figurine was found by a workman named either Johann Veran or Josef Veram

claims.claim: It was found on 7 August 1908 on a dig conducted by Josef Szombathy
claims.quote: It was recovered on 7 August 1908 on an archaeological dig conducted by Josef Szombathy, Hugo Obermaier, and Josef Bayer at a Paleolithic site near Willendorf, a village in Lower Austria.

claims.claim: 2022 research points to northern Italy near Lake Garda, across the Alps, as the closest and most likely source
claims.quote: Research published in 2022 indicates that the closest and most likely source of the oolite used is on the other side of the Alps in northern Italy, near Lake Garda.

claims.claim: A lesser candidate source is eastern Ukraine, about 1,600 km away
claims.quote: A lesser possibility is that it came from a site in eastern Ukraine some 1,600 km (1,000 mi) away.

claims.claim: The Ukrainian site is closer to southern Russian sites where similarly styled figurines have been found
claims.quote: the latter is closer to sites in southern Russia where similarly styled figurines have been found

claims.claim: The sourcing question raises questions about the mobility of ancient populations
claims.quote: In either case, this raises questions regarding the mobility of ancient populations.

claims.claim: She probably never had feet and could not stand on her own
claims.quote: Like other similar sculptures, it probably never had feet, and would not have stood on its own

claims.claim: She may have been pegged into soft ground
claims.quote: although it might have been pegged into soft ground

claims.claim: Both the fertility-goddess and self-portrait readings are speculative
claims.quote: As with similar figurines, evidence of the sculptor's intent is scant.

claims.claim: "Venus" is a modern label applied by archaeologists who assumed a fertility deity, and it postdates the carving by thousands of years
claims.quote: The reference to Venus is metaphorical, since the figurines predate the mythological figure of Venus by many thousands of years.

claims.claim: Some scholars instead call it the Woman from Willendorf
claims.quote: Some scholars reject this terminology, instead referring to the statuette as the Woman of or from Willendorf.

claims.claim: Catherine McCoid and LeRoy McDermott proposed the figurines were self-portraits, the body seen foreshortened from above, with the missing face explained by the absence of mirrors
claims.quote: Catherine McCoid and LeRoy McDermott hypothesize that the figurines may have been created as self-portraits by women. This theory stems from the correlation of the proportions of the statues to how the proportions of women's bodies would seem if they were looking down at themselves

claims.claim: Michael Bisson objected that pools and puddles work as mirrors
claims.quote: This reasoning has been criticized by McGill University anthropologist Michael S. Bisson, who notes that water pools and puddles would have been readily available natural mirrors for Paleolithic humans.
